strengths: MSAM addresses a practical limitation of SAM with a simple update that reuses momentum and requires one forward/backward pass per iteration. Table 1 reports approximately baseline training speed, compared with 0.52 times baseline speed for SAM.

The experiments show consistent improvements over base optimizers across CIFAR100 architectures and several ImageNet models. Equal-compute comparisons in Appendix A.8 strengthen the practical contribution, and adaptive and batch-normalization-only variants demonstrate compatibility with existing techniques.

The momentum-direction and normalization ablations provide useful empirical insights. In particular, the observation that negative stale momentum can increase loss, and the importance of separating perturbation magnitude from the learning-rate schedule, merit further investigation.

The update equations, schematic, repository link, training settings, and extensive hyperparameter sweeps aid understanding and reproducibility. The manuscript candidly documents instability and performance limitations. No material ethical concern is apparent from the reported work.
weaknesses: The theoretical support is invalid as stated. Proposition 1 fails for negative Hessian trace: with scalar Hessian H = -1 and standard Gaussian perturbations at rho = 1, its left side is approximately -0.199 while its right side is -1. Setting 1 does not require nonnegative trace. Theorem 3 also needs an explicit justification connecting perturbed population risk to unperturbed risk, appropriate loss and smoothness assumptions, and control of the Taylor remainder. The claim in Section 4.1 that improved generalization follows from this analysis is therefore unsupported.

The model-selection protocol leaves a significant evaluation ambiguity. Appendix A.15 reports the best rho from sweeps labeled as test accuracy, without specifying an independent validation selection procedure. Most ImageNet results are single runs; variability measured for smaller baseline models cannot establish uncertainty for other optimizers and architectures. The small translation improvement likewise lacks uncertainty estimates.

The SAM comparison uses unequal warm-up treatment. MSAM disables perturbations during warm-up, whereas the main SAM baseline retains them. Table A.2 shows that disabling them improves SAM from 69.2% to 69.8%, above MSAM's 69.1%. Moreover, Table 2 contains substantial SAM advantages, including 2.4 percentage points for ViT-S/16 at 300 epochs. Broader comparisons with matched schedules and computational budgets are needed to substantiate the claimed performance tradeoff.

Several mechanistic claims exceed the measurements. Section 4.2 compares gradients only after projecting MSAM's gradient into the SAM/SGD plane; agreement there can coexist with large orthogonal discrepancies. Full-vector similarities and residual norms are needed. Likewise, averaging gradients across changing parameter positions does not by itself establish an accurate approximation to the current full-dataset gradient.

The methodological novelty needs sharper positioning relative to NAG and extrapolation methods. Appendix A.2 finds normalization unnecessary, making independently scaled momentum extrapolation the central distinction. More explicit algorithmic comparisons with the cited extrapolation and momentum-based sharpness methods would clarify the advance. Combined with the proof and evaluation issues, the current evidence does not yet support acceptance.
